newsitem.title: UK: Platinum leads Ldn precious metals, gold firm.
newsitem.headline: Platinum leads Ldn precious metals, gold firm.

text.p: The price of platinum, squeezed by delays in Russian exports, extended gains on Monday with sister rare white metal palladium following up in its slipstream.

While dealers saw a potential in platinum to spiral $5-10 per ounce or more in a market awash with rumours on what Russia might do next, they said prices could collapse once shipments to the biggest market, Japan, resumed.
"The question is when to go short," said one European dealer.
"Hopefully we won't see the lows again (in platinum) but I think perhaps we are a bit...high," said another dealer.
By 1500 GMT platinum was $4.40 up at $381.90/2.90 an ounce.
Gold followed platinum early, but momentum stalled above $342 and dealers said attempts to push it higher would run into strong resistance at $345. Gold's fix was $342.25 from $342.15.
Prices did not budge on news the Russian central bank is planning to issue gold-backed bonds, but a dealer said, "If you securitise gold it's partly bullish because it can't be sold."
Dealers were puzzled about the significance of such plans after rumours of a Russian gold swap for platinum and palladium as collateral against a loan supposedly by the Swiss bank UBS.
"Obviously Russia needs additional gold, and if they can't get it from UBS they may have to buy some," said another dealer.
Forward platinum rates remained tight, with one-month lease rates hovering around 10 percent, but interest was clustered in short periods as players expected the pressure to ease soon.
"There is still tightness out there but immediately when we see liquidity get back into the market we will probably see platinum fall back about four, five dollars," said the dealer.
Last week spot platinum jumped from a low of $354 an ounce to $382.50 on Thursday following a spate of Swiss borrowing.
Palladium gained $4.25 on the back of platinum to $156.50 bid, but it was shy of challenging its recent high of $161.50.

Fuelling the market were perceptions that Russian exports, delayed since December, were nowhere near resumption as Moscow battled with bureaucratic snags and tried to overhaul its archaic precious metals market.
By 1500 GMT bullion was indicated at $342.10/$342.60 an once against Friday's close of $342.20/$$342.70.
"There may be attempts to try to push it down to the recent low of $336 and increases in open interest on Comex point to big short positions again," said a dealer.
Silver was static at around $4.75/$4.77 an ounce.
